n: Back in Capernaum, word spread quickly that Jesus was staying at a house — probably Peter’s home.

f.g: Reported, talked about.

n: So many people crowded in that even the doorway was blocked. Jesus used the moment to teach them God’s word.
Four friends carried a paralyzed man on a mat, hoping to bring him to Jesus.

f.g: Paralysis.
Carried by four men.

n: Blocked by the crowd, the friends climbed onto the flat roof, dug through it, and lowered their friend down. Village roofs were often beams covered with branches and packed clay.

f.g: Crowd, crush of people.

n: Jesus saw the friends’ faith and first addressed the man’s deepest need: forgiveness. Notice that other people’s faith helped bring this man to the Savior.
Some scribes in the room silently objected to what they had just heard.
Their reasoning was right that only God can forgive sins. Their mistake was failing to recognize that God was standing in front of them.

f.g: Speech that insults God or claims what belongs only to God.

f.w: who can forgive sins but God only?

n: Jesus knew what they were thinking without being told, and he answered their unspoken thoughts.
Anyone can claim to forgive sins — no one can see it. But a command to walk can be tested at once. Jesus was about to do the visible thing to prove the invisible one.

f.g: Which is easier.

n: The healing would show that Jesus, the “Son of Man,” truly had divine authority to forgive. Son of Man was Jesus’ favorite title for himself.

f.g: Jesus’ usual title for himself, drawn from Daniel’s vision; Latter-day Saint scripture links it to God, the “Man of Holiness.”

n: Jesus spoke directly to the paralyzed man: get up, pick up your mat, and go home.
The man stood up and walked out with everyone watching. The crowd praised God, saying they had never seen anything like it.

f.g: In this way, like this.

n: Jesus went back out to the lakeshore, and crowds came to him there to be taught.
Levi (also called Matthew) collected taxes for the Roman-backed rulers. Tax collectors were often despised, yet Jesus invited him to follow, and Levi got up and did.

f.g: A tax booth, where duties on goods were collected.

n: Levi held a meal in his home, and many tax collectors and other people with bad reputations ate with Jesus and his disciples.

f.g: Reclined at a meal; guests lay on couches around a low table.
Tax collectors, seen as collaborators with Rome and often as cheats.

n: Religious leaders were shocked. Sharing a meal signaled friendship and acceptance, and they thought a holy man should keep away from sinners.

f.g: A Jewish group known for strict observance of the law and traditions.

n: Jesus compared himself to a doctor. A doctor goes to the sick, not the healthy. He came to call people who know they need help to repent and be healed.
Followers of John the Baptist and the Pharisees fasted regularly, and people asked why Jesus’ disciples didn’t.

f.g: Go without food (and drink) for a time, usually for religious devotion or mourning.

n: Jesus compared his presence to a wedding. Guests don’t fast while the groom is at the celebration — it’s a time for joy.

f.g: Wedding guests, especially the groom’s close friends.

n: A quiet hint of his coming death: when the groom is taken away, then his friends will fast and mourn.
A patch of new, unshrunk cloth will shrink and tear an old garment. Jesus’ gospel couldn’t simply be stitched onto old traditions.

f.g: Tear.

n: Wine was stored in leather skins. New wine expands as it ferments; an old, stiff skin would burst. The new life Jesus brings needs new, flexible hearts.

f.g: Wineskins — leather bags, not glass bottles.

n: Walking through grain fields on the sabbath, the disciples picked heads of grain to eat. Picking by hand from a neighbor’s field was allowed by the law.

f.g: In KJV English, any grain — here wheat or barley, not American maize.

n: The Pharisees counted plucking and rubbing grain as harvesting — forbidden work on the sabbath under their traditions.
Jesus answered from scripture, reminding them of a time when hungry David and his men did something normally not allowed.

f.g: Hungry.

n: David ate the holy bread set out in the sanctuary, which only priests were meant to eat. Human need was put first. (The priest in 1 Samuel is Abiathar’s father, Ahimelech.)

f.g: Twelve loaves set before the Lord each sabbath in the tabernacle, later eaten by priests.

n: God gave the sabbath as a blessing for people — a day of rest and worship — not as a burden to enslave them.

f.w: The sabbath was made for man

n: As the one who gave the sabbath in the first place, Jesus has authority over how it should be kept.

f.g: The JST adds that the sabbath was given as a day of rest and that man was made to glorify God.
